version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm: madvise: drop MADV_PAGEOUT folios at swap writeback completion

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch improves the handling of MADV_PAGEOUT folios on asynchronous swap devices by marking them as dropbehind at isolation time instead of waiting for writeback completion. This allows the memory to be freed earlier, reducing latency and improving performance. The patch also updates various kernel modules to handle the new behavior correctly.

review_comments.author: David (Arm)
review_comments.summary: Reviewer David (Arm) pointed out that the patch's behavior for MADV_PAGEOUT is inconsistent with synchronous I/O, where memory is released immediately after sync I/O completion. He argued that delaying the release until a later scan may improve swapcache hits before folios are reclaimed, but questioned whether this is relevant in practice and suggested that evicting pages as soon as possible would be more beneficial for freeing up memory.
review_comments.raw_body:
On 9/21/26 17:24, Alexandre Ghiti wrote:
> On an asynchronous swap device MADV_PAGEOUT only marks the folio
> PG_reclaim and rotates it to the tail of the inactive list once its
> writeback completes, so the memory is not actually freed until a later
> reclaim scan removes the by then clean swap cache folio.
But we have the same behavior when just reclaiming memory ordinarily? It's added
to the swapcache and only the next scan actually frees up the memory.

Wouldn't we memory we reclaim ... just gone, like in the sync case?

-- 
Cheers,

David

review_comments.author: Barry Song
review_comments.summary: Barry Song noted that asynchronous swap devices can experience a cold/hot inversion when rotating writeback folios to the tail of the inactive list due to fast NVMe I/O, where some pages complete writeback during isolation while others remain under writeback. He suggested skipping the later scan and reclaiming the folios immediately once the I/O completes for MADV_PAGEOUT, which is an explicit hint from userspace to reclaim memory.

On Mon, Sep 21, 2026 at 11:37 PM David Hildenbrand (Arm)
<david@kernel.org> wrote:
>
> On 9/21/26 17:24, Alexandre Ghiti wrote:
> > On an asynchronous swap device MADV_PAGEOUT only marks the folio
> > PG_reclaim and rotates it to the tail of the inactive list once its
> > writeback completes, so the memory is not actually freed until a later
> > reclaim scan removes the by then clean swap cache folio.
> But we have the same behavior when just reclaiming memory ordinarily? It's added
> to the swapcache and only the next scan actually frees up the memory.
>
> Wouldn't we memory we reclaim ... just gone, like in the sync case?

For synchronous I/O, such as zswap and zram, the memory is released
immediately after sync I/O is done.

For asynchronous I/O, such as NVMe, the swapcache is currently
expected to be rotated back to the tail of the LRU and wait for
another scan. Alexandre once mentioned that when he tried handling
async I/O the same way as sync I/O—releasing the memory once the I/O
completed—he saw some regression. So, delaying the release until a
later scan may allow swapcache hits before the folios are eventually
reclaimed.

But we actually have a problem here: this rotation, which puts
writeback folios at the tail of the LRU, is not reliable at all.

`folio_rotate_reclaimable()` would only work reliably if the endio
happens after the folio has been put back on the LRU head, rather than
while it is still isolated.

But nowadays NVMe is very fast. If we isolate N pages and perform
shrink on them, M pages may finish writeback during the isolation,
while the remaining N-M pages are still under writeback. M can easily
be more than 50% of N.

As a result, we can end up with the following cold/hot inversion:

LRU head
----- M pages whose writeback completed during isolation
----- other pages
----- N-M pages that are successfully rotated to the LRU tail
LRU tail

Now we can see that the M pages were expected to be reclaimed, but
they are not only left unreclaimed, but are effectively promoted to
the LRU head.

For MGLRU, commit 359a5e1416ca ("mm: multi-gen LRU: retry folios
written back while isolated") added the following code to reclaim
those M pages that finish writeback during isolation by retrying
`shrink_folio_list()` on them:

                /* retry folios that may have missed
folio_rotate_reclaimable() */
                if (!skip_retry && !folio_test_active(folio) &&
!folio_mapped(folio) &&
                    !folio_test_dirty(folio) && !folio_test_writeback(folio)) {
                        list_move(&folio->lru, &clean);
                        continue;
                }

This somehow resolves the cold/hot inversion, but leaves the M and
N-M pages with inconsistent behavior: some are actually reclaimed,
while others remain at the tail of the LRU.

For the active/inactive LRU and `MADV_PAGEOUT`, we don't have a
mechanism to restore the missed reclaim opportunity. Ridong's patch[1]
addresses this cold/hot inversion in the active/inactive LRU reclaim
path. To my knowledge, there has never been a patch to address the
same cold/hot inversion in `MADV_PAGEOUT`.

BTW, if `MADV_PAGEOUT` is an explicit hint from userspace to reclaim
the memory, would it make sense to skip the later scan and reclaim the
folios immediately once the I/O completes?

[1] https://lore.kernel.org/linux-mm/20260920132519.3369946-1-ridong.chen@linux.dev/

Best Regards
Barry

> But we actually have a problem here: this rotation, which puts
> writeback folios at the tail of the LRU, is not reliable at all.
>
> `folio_rotate_reclaimable()` would only work reliably if the endio
> happens after the folio has been put back on the LRU head, rather than
> while it is still isolated.

I think we might better fix this instead? Or is this really a problem?
If it has PG_reclaim, it should be putback to the tail instead of
head, right?

> But nowadays NVMe is very fast. If we isolate N pages and perform
> shrink on them, M pages may finish writeback during the isolation,
> while the remaining N-M pages are still under writeback. M can easily
> be more than 50% of N.
>
> As a result, we can end up with the following cold/hot inversion:
>
> LRU head
> ----- M pages whose writeback completed during isolation
> ----- other pages
> ----- N-M pages that are successfully rotated to the LRU tail
> LRU tail
>
> Now we can see that the M pages were expected to be reclaimed, but
> they are not only left unreclaimed, but are effectively promoted to
> the LRU head.
>

> written back while isolated") added the following code to reclaim
> those M pages that finish writeback during isolation by retrying
> `shrink_folio_list()` on them:
>
>                 /* retry folios that may have missed
> folio_rotate_reclaimable() */
>                 if (!skip_retry && !folio_test_active(folio) &&
> !folio_mapped(folio) &&
>                     !folio_test_dirty(folio) && !folio_test_writeback(folio)) {
>                         list_move(&folio->lru, &clean);
>                         continue;
>                 }
>
> This somehow resolves the cold/hot inversion, but leaves the M and
> N-M pages with inconsistent behavior: some are actually reclaimed,
> while others remain at the tail of the LRU.
>
> For the active/inactive LRU and `MADV_PAGEOUT`, we don't have a
> mechanism to restore the missed reclaim opportunity. Ridong's patch[1]
> addresses this cold/hot inversion in the active/inactive LRU reclaim
> path. To my knowledge, there has never been a patch to address the
> same cold/hot inversion in `MADV_PAGEOUT`.

MADV_PAGEOUT is a bit different from the reclaim under pressure,
reclaim underpressure can easily overshoot the amount of anon folios
reclaimed, because however fast the writeback it, it can be faster by
scanning the LRU and dropping clean file folios. So before LRU
reclaimed enough clean file folios, we can't stop the reclaim.

I think the better fix is to have a separate watermark for anon / file
or a new way to handle reclaim. Reclaiming an anon folio is hardly
helpful in the short term when under heavy pressure and the device is
not a synchronous device.

The overshoot is a real issue, it's very common to see many folios
stuck in the swap cache after memory pressure. If we drop all of them,
we will see significant regressions. Treating MADV_PAGEOUT differently
here seems better.

> > >>>

> > >
> > >>
> > >> Right. But these would happen in both the SYNC and the ASYNC case. Which seems

> > >>
> > >> Or is the SYNC case in general so fast that it is not a problem and the

> > >
> > > I think the problem is not LRU being inaccurate, but ASYNC case could
> > > overshoot the anon reclaim very easily. File folios can be simply
> > > dropped, and increase nr_reclaimed, but anon writeback (swap) can't be

> > :D
> >
> > >
> > >>

> > >>> Even on Android, which uses zram with very fast synchronous swap-out,
> > >>> I can still hit the swapcache from time to time. So perhaps with a
> > >>> slower device, such as an HDD, keeping the swapcache around for longer
> > >>> could allow applications to hit it more often?
> > >>
> > >> Why is that specific for HDD? It's the exact same app behavior independent of
> > >> the underlying swap technology.
> > >
> > > If you have a shared folio, you must use swap cache, and even for
> > > single used folios swap cache is the way to do synchronization,
> > > regardless of the device.
> > >
> > >>>
> > >>> I don't know. Maybe Alexandre can share more details about this
> > >>> benchmark. I'm also a little surprised by the 15% regression in
> > >>> Sysbench OLTP. My initial feeling was the same as yours: we should
> > >>> release the memory immediately after writeback completes, for both
> > >>> synchronous and asynchronous I/O.
> > >>
> > >> Right. And see if we can identify why we are swapping out the wrong things :)
> > >

Alex, One question about the `nr_reclaimed` accounting.

`PAGE_DROPBEHIND` increments `nr_reclaimed` when the write is
submitted, while the folio may still be under writeback and is only
actually removed from the swap cache when writeback completes.

Kairui pointed out that async swap can over-reclaim because
`nr_reclaimed` does not increase while anon folios remain under
writeback. Does the early accounting for `PAGE_DROPBEHIND` address
that over-reclaim mechanism for this `MADV_PAGEOUT` path?

It might also be useful to check this with a delayed swap device, such
as the `dm-delay` case Kairui mentioned.

Thanks,
Kunwu

series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames a local variable in the alloc_pages_bulk_noprof function to clarify its scope and purpose. The variable, previously named alloc_flags, is used for fast-path watermark, cpuset, and CMA decisions, which are distinct from the allocator behavior flags stored in the alloc_context. The renaming does not change the functionality of the code, but improves clarity by distinguishing between these two types of flags.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 2/6] mm/page_alloc: refactor alloc_flags preparation
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the preparation of allocation flags in the Linux kernel's page allocator. It moves the setup of ALLOC_NOLOCK and its associated watermark into a new function called prepare_alloc_flags(), which is then called from both alloc_frozen_pages_noprof() and alloc_pages_bulk_noprof(). The bulk allocator continues to use ALLOC_DEFAULT. This change does not alter the functionality of the code, but rather simplifies it by reducing duplication.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 3/6] mm/page_alloc: add an alloc_flags-aware folio allocator
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds an alloc_flags-aware folio allocator to the Linux kernel's page allocation system, allowing for more flexible and customizable memory allocation behavior. The existing exported folio and node interfaces remain unchanged, with ALLOC_DEFAULT being used as a wrapper. This change is intended to provide a low-level interface that can be used internally by the MM subsystem without affecting external users of the folio allocator.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 4/6] mm/mempolicy: plumb alloc_flags through folio allocation
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds an alloc_flags argument to the MM-internal policy allocator and carries it through preferred-many, huge-page, and general policy allocation paths in the NUMA policy allocation code. The public mempolicy folio interface remains as an ALLOC_DEFAULT wrapper. Non-task requests bypass task policy selection and use the supplied preferred node directly. No existing caller behavior is changed.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 5/6] mm/filemap: plumb alloc_flags through folio allocation
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds an internal filemap folio allocator that accepts and preserves explicit allocator behavior flags (alloc_flags) across allocation paths in the mm/filemap module. The existing filemap_alloc_folio_noprof function is modified to accept alloc_flags, allowing MM-internal callers to preserve these flags. This change does not introduce any functional changes but provides a way for internal callers to control allocator behavior. The patch includes modifications to several functions within the mm/filemap.c file and introduces new inline functions to handle allocation with specific flags.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 6/6] mm/page_alloc: let the bulk allocator carry alloc_flags
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new function __alloc_pages_bulk_noprof() in the Linux kernel's page allocation module, which allows callers to specify allocator behavior flags. The existing alloc_pages_bulk_noprof() function is modified to use this new function and pass default flags. This change enables internal MM callers to select specific behaviors through the bulk interface, addressing a limitation in the original implementation.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This RFC patch series aims to pass allocator flags through the folio, filemap, and bulk allocation interfaces in the Linux kernel. The current implementation hardcodes ALLOC_DEFAULT before reaching the page allocator, which can lead to conflicts between multiple MM series. This series separates allocator behavior flags from bulk allocator fast-path flags and shares their validation and preparation.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/2] mm: refactor find_next_best_node to find_next_best_node_in
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the find_next_best_node function to make it more flexible by allowing it to take an explicit list of candidate nodes instead of always using the N_MEMORY set. This change enables building fallback lists with non-N_MEMORY candidates, but does not introduce any functional changes as all callers still select from N_MEMORY. The refactor is done in three files: mm/internal.h, mm/memory-tiers.c, and mm/page_alloc.c.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/2] mm/page_alloc: refactor build_node_zonelist() out of build_zonelists()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the build_node_zonelist() function out of build_zonelists(). It extracts per-node fallback-list construction into a separate function, allowing new zonelists to be built from candidate nodemasks instead of just the default N_MEMORY node state list. The patch also adds a zlidx argument to callers so they can explicitly select the destination zonelist. This change does not introduce any functional changes and maintains the same fallback list as before.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch refactors the zonelist constructors and iterators in the Linux kernel to make them more flexible and modular. It introduces a new function `find_next_best_node_in` that takes an explicit candidate set, allowing callers to narrow down the selection of nodes. Additionally, it extracts a per-node construction loop from `build_zonelists` into a separate function `build_node_zonelist`, parameterized on the candidate nodemask and destination zonelist index. These changes enable building and iterating over zonelists for specific sets of nodes, which is a prerequisite for generating private node zonelists.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 01/10] selftests/mm: exercise MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds self-tests to exercise the MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT functionality in the Linux kernel. The tests cover both user-visible contracts, such as verifying that MADV_COLD does not populate PTE holes and that PAGEOUT preserves unevictable base pages, as well as implementation details like folio and page-table behavior under various scenarios. The patch includes 28 cases to test these behaviors, with some tests intentionally asserting specific conditions to detect unintended changes during a planned refactor of the page-table walker.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 06/10] mm/madvise: separate huge PMDs from the PTE walk
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the handling of huge PMDs from the PTE walk in the madvise_lru_pmd_entry function. It introduces a new helper function, madvise_lru_huge_pmd, which is responsible for handling huge PMDs and returns false when a requested split requires a PTE walk. The patch moves the lock ownership and splitting of huge PMDs into this dedicated helper, making the code more modular and easier to understand.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 07/10] mm/madvise: separate PTE-batch folio processing
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the processing of PTE-batch folios into a new helper function, madvise_lru_pte_batch_locked(). This function takes care of locking and referencing a split candidate folio before returning it to the caller. The original code combined page-table iteration with validation and processing in a single loop, which made it difficult to understand the batching rules for large folios and the ownership transferred when a partial folio is split. By moving this logic into a separate function, the patch improves the clarity and maintainability of the code without introducing any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 08/10] mm/madvise: separate the PTL-held PTE scan
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the PTE scan in the madvise function from its surrounding lock drops, allowing it to run entirely under the PTE lock. The scan is moved into a helper function that returns a locked and referenced split candidate or stops at the existing scheduling boundary. This change does not introduce any functional changes but improves the code's structure and efficiency.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 09/10] mm/madvise: make cold and pageout PTE lock ownership explicit
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the madvise_lru_pte_range_locked function to explicitly manage PTE lock ownership, making it clear who holds the lock during page-walking and huge PMD handling. The original code mixed lock ownership between the PMD callback and the page-walk callback, which is now separated into two distinct functions. This change does not introduce any functional changes but improves the clarity of the code by explicitly managing lock ownership.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 10/10] mm/madvise: share cold and pageout walk setup
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the shared TLB and page-walk setup for MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT operations in the Linux kernel's mm/madvise module. It introduces a new helper function, madvise_lru_vma_range(), which is used by both entry points to perform the common setup tasks. The patch aims to reduce code duplication and improve maintainability without introducing any functional changes.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch refactors the code responsible for handling MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT page table walks to improve maintainability and auditability. The original implementation was a complex nest of functions, which led to bugs being introduced frequently. To address this issue, the patch separates the handling of huge PMDs, PTE batching, PTE-lock ownership, and shared walk setup into distinct functions. Additionally, 28 self-tests are included to ensure that the refactored code does not introduce new issues. The patch aims to simplify the control flow and make it easier to audit page-table lock ownership and split retries.

version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm/page_alloc: let the bulk and folio allocators carry alloc_flags

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch allows the bulk and folio allocators to carry allocation flags, enabling callers to select allocator behavior such as an alternate zonelist. The change adds new entry points in page_alloc.h that take an explicit alloc_flags parameter, matching the existing __alloc_pages_noprof() function. This modification does not introduce any functional changes, as all current callers pass ALLOC_DEFAULT. The patch is a preparatory step to address potential conflicts with other ongoing work on allocation flags.

Sashiko pointed out some issues that arise from rebasing on the recent
ALLOC_NOLOCK work, and in a quick review I found a similar slow-path
fallback issue with the NOBLOCK patch separate of this patch.

review_comments.author: Lance Yang
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Lance Yang noted that __alloc_pages_bulk_noprof() can bypass the alloc_nolock_allowed() check and reach critical sections without verifying if locking is allowed, potentially causing a lock ordering violation.
review_comments.raw_body:
Yeah, but what if a caller passes ALLOC_NOLOCK in the future?

__alloc_pages_noprof() checks alloc_nolock_allowed() first, but
__alloc_pages_bulk_noprof() can enter its fast path without that check.

That fast path can reach _deferred_grow_zone() or pcp_spin_trylock().
Shouldn't we do the same check first?

Or am I missing something?

Cheers, Lance

review_comments.raw_body:

this issue up and I've been poking at it.

I've actually been reworking this patch and pulled in changes from the
ALLOC_UNMAPPED series to address this all at once.  I've been developing
a page allocator unit-testing harness to help validate some assumptions
before I post it.

~Gregory

It's not necessary for bulk alloc to support ALLOC_NOLOCK just because it
takes flags. e.g. kmalloc_nolock() supports a subset of gfp flags as well.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/3] mm/huge_memory: make thp_underused() work for mTHP folios
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the thp_underused() function to make it work with mTHP folios, which are larger than PMD-sized folios. The function is made size-aware instead of hardcoded to PMD-sized folios. A new helper function, thp_can_be_underused(), is introduced to check if a folio can be underused based on the number of zero-filled pages and the sysctl maximum value. This change will allow anonymous mTHP folios to be added to the deferred split list in future patches.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/3] mm/huge_memory: don't queue folios that can never be underused
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the handling of anonymous PMD-sized folios in the Linux kernel by skipping the queuing of folios that can never be underused, reducing unnecessary work and improving performance. The default khugepaged/max_ptes_none setting causes the shrinker to never split these folios for being underused, so they are not queued. This change is particularly important for a subsequent patch that adds anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list, as it prevents small mTHP orders from taking the list_lru lock on every anonymous fault.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/3] mm/memory: add anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds anonymous mTHP (huge page) folios to the deferred split list in the Linux kernel's memory management code. This allows for underused splitting of huge pages, which can help reclaim unused parts of large memory allocations when the system is under memory pressure. The patch addresses a problem where fully mapped huge pages that are mostly zero-filled do not get split by the deferred split shrinker, leading to memory regressions. The solution involves mirroring the behavior for PMD-sized folios and adding a check to minimize overhead on common fault paths.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses memory regressions caused by enabling 2M THP=always on arm64 with 64k base pages. The patches split underused anonymous mTHP folios, which are not currently reclaimed under memory pressure. Patch 1 makes the thp_underused() function size-aware to accommodate larger folio sizes. Patch 2 optimizes existing behavior by keeping folios that can never be found underused off the deferred split queue. Patch 3 queues anonymous mTHP folios from map_anon_folio_pte_nopf(), mirroring what is already done for PMD folios. The patches aim to provide a solution for deploying 2M THP=always on arm64 without causing memory regressions.

The creep problem was discussed plenty of times. That's when we decided to start

which use cases would need them.  Without support for deferred shrinker, there
wasn't really the need to support other values.

Some of it can be had in:

commit 5a9c05d86683db5449b7fefd278c461cffb55234
Author: Nico Pache <nico.pache@linux.dev>
Date:   Fri Jun 5 10:14:11 2026 -0600

    mm/khugepaged: generalize __collapse_huge_page_* for mTHP support

    generalize the order of the __collapse_huge_page_* and collapse_max_*
    functions to support future mTHP collapse.

    The current mechanism for determining collapse with the
    khugepaged_max_ptes_none value is not designed with mTHP in mind.  This
    raises a key design issue: if we support user defined max_pte_none values
    (even those scaled by order), a collapse of a lower order can introduces
    an feedback loop, or "creep", when max_ptes_none is set to a value greater
    than HPAGE_PMD_NR / 2.  [1]

    With this configuration, a successful collapse to order N will populate
    enough pages to satisfy the collapse condition on order N+1 on the next
    scan.  This leads to unnecessary work and memory churn.

    To fix this issue introduce a helper function that will limit mTHP
    collapse support to two max_ptes_none values, 0 and HPAGE_PMD_NR - 1.
    This effectively supports two modes: [2]

    - max_ptes_none=0: never collapses if it encounters an empty PTE or a PTE
      that maps the shared zeropage. Consequently, no memory bloat.
    - max_ptes_none=511 (on 4k pagesz): Always collapse to the highest
      available mTHP order.

    This removes the possibility of "creep", and a warning will be emitted if
    any non-supported max_ptes_none value is configured with mTHP enabled.
    Any intermediate value will default mTHP collapse to max_ptes_none=0.

    mTHP collapse will not honor the khugepaged_max_ptes_shared or
    khugepaged_max_ptes_swap parameters, and will fail if it encounters a
    shared or swapped entry.


Tracing back the discussion on that patch should give you all the details.

Cheers,

David

<david@kernel.org> wrote:

in the non-default max_ptes_none case, since any folio can now
potentially qualify as underused. This drew some objections in v1,

out scaling. The objections were a) the list_lru lock contention and
b) the limited upside vs cost of splitting small folios.

problem. If it would be helpful to have some benchmark numbers, I'm
happy to run a synthetic one (patch 3 applied (which adds anon mTHP
folios to the deferred split list), only order-2 enabled,

anonymous mapping). I'm happy to run something else if anyone has a
